OPD-V: Visual On-Policy Self-Distillation with Modality Balance

Visual teacher contrasts select self-distillation tokens that receive stronger support from the image.

Aniri

August 5, 2026 ·Preprint ·3-minute read ·Read the paper ·PDF ·Code
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

OPD-V examines modality imbalance in visual on-policy self-distillation. A teacher can be confident while relying mainly on textual context, leaving the additional visual information underused. The method contrasts a zoom-in positive teacher with an image-masked negative teacher under matched text and student-generated prefixes.

Their token-logit margin defines a modality-balance trust region. Distillation focuses on tokens for which the positive visual condition supplies stronger support, connecting the selection of supervision to evidence use rather than treating every confident teacher output equally.

6Evaluation benchmarks
4Multimodal backbones
5Post-training methods

A useful distillation signal should reward how a teacher uses visual evidence, alongside what it predicts.

Why this matters

Privileged information improves training only when the teacher effectively uses it. In a multimodal model, confidence and correctness alone may not reveal whether an apparent reasoning signal depends on the image.

How it works

  1. Score the same student-generated tokens with the original-image student, zoom-in positive teacher, and masked-image negative teacher.
  2. Use positive modality-balance logit margins to select an on-policy trust region.
  3. Apply Jensen–Shannon self-distillation from the positive teacher on the selected tokens and compare quality and training cost.

What the study finds

Experiments span six benchmarks, four multimodal backbones, and five post-training methods. Analyses compare attention balance and teacher behavior, training dynamics, component ablations, and wall-clock step time. The reported results support the proposed supervision-selection criterion in those settings.

What this means

The work treats the quality of supervision as partly a question of information dependence. Contrasting visual conditions helps identify where a teacher’s support is associated with richer visual input, providing a practical way to use that distinction during training.

This connects evaluation and optimization: a diagnostic of modality use becomes a criterion for selecting which updates to trust. The larger question is when that criterion continues to track genuinely useful evidence across image transformations, tasks, and model families.
